Selective review of offline change point detection methods

Journal: Signal Processing
Charles Truong Address: CMLA, CNRS, ENS Paris Saclay Corresponding author: Corresponding author     Laurent Oudre Address: L2TI, University Paris 13     Nicolas Vayatis Address: CMLA, CNRS, ENS Paris Saclay
Abstract

This article presents a selective survey of algorithms for the offline detection of multiple change points in multivariate time series. A general yet structuring methodological strategy is adopted to organize this vast body of work. More precisely, detection algorithms considered in this review are characterized by three elements: a cost function, a search method and a constraint on the number of changes. Each of those elements is described, reviewed and discussed separately. Implementations of the main algorithms described in this article are provided within a Python package called ruptures.

Keywords: 
change point detection, segmentation, statistical signal processing

1 Introduction

A common task in signal processing is the identification and analysis of complex systems whose underlying state changes, possibly several times. This setting arises when industrial systems, physical phenomena or human activity are continuously monitored with sensors. The objective of practitioners is to extract from the recorded signals a posteriori meaningful information about the different states and transitions of the monitored object for analysis purposes. This setting encompasses a broad range of real-world scenarios and a wide variety of signals.

Change point detection is the task of finding changes in the underlying model of a signal or time series. The first works on change point detection go back to the 50s Page [1954], Page [1955]: the goal was to locate a shift in the mean of independent and identically distributed (iid) Gaussian variables for industrial quality control purposes. Since then, this problem has been actively investigated, and is periodically the subject of in-depth monographs Basseville and Nikiforov [1993], Brodsky and Darkhovsky [1993], Csörgö and Horváth [1997], Chen and Gupta [2011a]. This subject has generated important activity in statistics and signal processing [Lavielle and Teyssière, 2007, Jandhyala et al., 2013, Haynes et al., 2017a] but also in various application settings such as speech processing Desobry et al. [2005], Harchaoui et al. [2009], Angelosante and Giannakis [2012], Seichepine et al. [2014], financial analysis Lavielle and Teyssière [2007], Bai and Perron [1998], Frick et al. [2014], bio-informatics Hocking et al. [2013a], Maidstone et al. [2017], Vert and Bleakley [2010], Picard et al. [2005], Guédon [2013], Chakar et al. [2017], Oudre et al. [2015], Audiffren et al. [2015], Liu et al. [2018], climatology Maidstone [2013], Verbesselt et al. [2010], Reeves et al. [2007], network traffic data analysis Lévy-Leduc and Roueff [2009], Lung-Yut-Fong et al. [2012]. Modern applications in bioinformatics, finance, monitoring of complex systems have also motivated recent developments from the machine learning community [Vert and Bleakley, 2010, Lajugie et al., 2014, Hocking et al., 2015].

Let us take the example of gait analysis, illustrated on the flowchart displayed on Figure 1. In this context, a patient’s movements are monitored with accelerometers and gyroscopes while performing simple activities, for instance walking at preferred speed, running or standing still. The objective is to objectively quantify gait characteristics Barrois-Müller et al. [2016a], Barrois-Müller et al. [2016b], Oudre et al. [2018], Truong et al. [2015], Barrois-Müller et al. [2015]. The resulting signal is described as a succession of non-overlapping segments, each one corresponding to an activity and having its own gait characteristics. Insightful features from homogeneous phases can be extracted if the temporal boundaries of those segments are identified. This analysis therefore needs a preliminary processing of the signals: change point detection.

Change point detection methods are divided into two main branches: online methods, that aim to detect changes as soon as they occur in a real-time setting, and offline methods that retrospectively detect changes when all samples are received. The former task is often referred to as event or anomaly detection, while the latter is sometimes called signal segmentation.

In this article, we propose a survey of algorithms for the detection of multiple change points in multivariate time series. All reviewed methods presented in this paper address the problem of offline (also referred to as retrospective or a posteriori) change point detection, in which segmentation is performed after the signal has been collected. The objective of this article is to facilitate the search of a suitable detection method for a given application. In particular, focus is made on practical considerations such as implementations and procedures to calibrate the algorithms. This review also presents the mathematical properties of the main approaches, as well as the metrics to evaluate and compare their results. This article is linked with a Python scientific library called ruptures Truong [2018], that includes a modular and easy-to-use implementation of all the main methods presented in this paper.

2 Background

This section introduces the main concepts for change point detection, as well as the selection criteria and the outline of this review.

2.1 Notations

In the remainder of this article, we use the following notations. For a given signal y={yt}t=1Ty=\{y_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, the (b−a)(b-a)-sample long sub-signal {yt}t=a+1b\{y_{t}\}_{t=a+1}^{b} (1≤a<b≤T1\leq a<b\leq T) is simply denoted ya..by_{a..b}; the complete signal is therefore y=y0..Ty=y_{0..T}. A set of indexes is denoted by a calligraphic letter: 𝒯={t1,t2,…}⊂{1,…,T}\mathcal{T}=\{t_{1},t_{2},\dots\}\subset\{1,\dots,T\}, and its cardinal is |𝒯||\mathcal{T}|. For a set of indexes 𝒯={t1,…,tK}\mathcal{T}=\{t_{1},\dots,t_{K}\}, the dummy indexes t0:=0t_{0}:=0 and tK+1:=Tt_{K+1}:=T are implicitly available.

2.2 Problem formulation

Let us consider a multivariate non-stationary random process y={y1,…,yT}y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{T}\} that takes value in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (d≥1d\geq 1) and has TT samples. The signal yy is assumed to be piecewise stationary, meaning that some characteristics of the process change abruptly at some unknown instants t1∗<t2∗<⋯<tK∗∗t^{*}_{1}<t^{*}_{2}<\dots<t^{*}_{K^{*}}. Change point detection consists in estimating the indexes tk∗t^{*}_{k}. Depending on the context, the number K∗K^{*} of changes may or may not be known, in which case it has to be estimated too.

Formally, change point detection is cast as a model selection problem, which consists in choosing the best possible segmentation 𝒯\mathcal{T} according to a quantitative criterion V⁡(𝒯,y)V(\mathcal{T},y) that must be minimized. (The function V⁡(𝒯,y)V(\mathcal{T},y) is simply denoted V⁡(𝒯)V(\mathcal{T}) when it is obvious from the context that it refers to the signal yy.) The choice of the criterion function V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot) depends on preliminary knowledge on the task at hand.

In this work, we make the assumption that the criterion function V⁡(𝒯)V(\mathcal{T}) for a particular segmentation is a sum of costs of all the segments that define the segmentation:

V⁡(𝒯,y):=∑k=0Kc⁡(ytk..tk+1)V(\mathcal{T},y):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}\ c(y_{t_{k}..t_{k+1}}) (1)

where c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot) is a cost function which measures goodness-of-fit of the sub-signal ytk..tk+1={yt}tk+1tk+1y_{t_{k}..t_{k+1}}=\{y_{t}\}_{t_{k}+1}^{t_{k+1}} to a specific model. The “best segmentation” 𝒯^\widehat{\mathcal{T}} is the minimizer of the criterion V⁡(𝒯)V(\mathcal{T}). In practice, depending on whether the number K∗K^{*} of change points is known beforehand, change point detection methods fall into two categories.

  • •

    Problem 1 : known number of changes KK. The change point detection problem with a fixed number KK of change points consists in solving the following discrete optimization problem

    min|𝒯|=K⁡V⁡(𝒯).\min_{|\mathcal{T}|=K}\ V(\mathcal{T}). (P1)
  • •

    Problem 2 : unknown number of changes. The change point detection problem with an unknown number of change points consists in solving the following discrete optimization problem

    min𝒯⁡V⁡(𝒯)+pen​(𝒯)\min_{\mathcal{T}}\ V(\mathcal{T})\ +\ \mbox{pen}(\mathcal{T}) (P2)

    where pen​(𝒯)\mbox{pen}(\mathcal{T}) is an appropriate measure of the complexity of a segmentation 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

All change point detection methods considered in this work yield an exact or an approximate solution to either Problem 1 (P1) or Problem 2 (P2), with the function V⁡(𝒯,y)V(\mathcal{T},y) adhering to the format (1).

2.3 Selection criteria for the review

To better understand the strengths and weaknesses of change point detection methods, we propose to classify algorithms according to a comprehensive typology. Precisely, detection methods are expressed as the combination of the following three elements.

  • •

    Cost function. The cost function c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot) is a measure of “homogeneity”. Its choice encodes the type of changes that can be detected. Intuitively, c⁡(ya..b)c(y_{a..b}) is expected to be low if the sub-signal ya..by_{a..b} is “homogeneous” (meaning that it does not contain any change point), and large if the sub-signal ya..by_{a..b} is “heterogeneous” (meaning that it contains one or several change points).

  • •

    Search method. The search method is the resolution procedure for the discrete optimization problems associated with Problem 1 (P1) and Problem 2 (P2). The literature contains several methods to efficiently solve those problems, in an exact fashion or in an approximate fashion. Each method strikes a balance between computational complexity and accuracy.

  • •

    Constraint (on the number of change points). When the number of changes is unknown (P2), a constraint is added, in the form of a complexity penalty pen​(⋅)\mbox{pen}(\cdot) (P2), to balance out the goodness-of-fit term V⁡(𝒯,y)V(\mathcal{T},y). The choice of the complexity penalty is related to the amplitude of the changes to detect: with too “small” a penalty (compared to the goodness-of-fit) in (P2), many change points are detected, even those that are the result of noise. Conversely, too much penalization only detects the most significant changes, or even none.

This typology of change point detection methods is schematically shown on Figure 2.

2.4 Limitations

The described framework, however general, does not encompass all published change point detection methods. In particular, Bayesian approaches are not considered in the remainder of this article, even though they provide state-of-the-art results in several domains, such as speech and sound processing. The most well-known Bayesian algorithm is the Hidden Markov Model (HMM) Rabiner [1989]. This model was later extended, for instance with Dirichlet processes Ko et al. [2015], Martínez and Mena [2014] or product partition models Barry and Hartigan [1992], Barry and Hartigan [1993]. The interested reader can find reviews of Bayesian approaches in Brodsky and Darkhovsky [1993] and Chen and Gupta [2011a].
Also, several literature reviews with different selection criteria can be found. Recent and important works include Aminikhanghahi and Cook [2017] which focuses on window-based detection algorithms. In particular, the authors use the quantity of samples needed to detect a change as a basis for comparison. Maximum likelihood and Bayes-type detection are reviewed, from a theoretical standpoint, in Jandhyala et al. [2013]. Existing asymptotic distributions for change point estimates are described for several statistical models. In Niu et al. [2016], detection is formulated as a statistical hypothesis testing problem, and emphasis is put on the algorithmic and theoretical properties of several sequential mean-shift detection procedures.

2.5 Outline of the article

Before starting this review, we propose in Section 3 a detailed overview of the main mathematical tools that can be used for evaluating and comparing the change point detection methods. The organization of the remaining of this review article reflects the typology of change point detection methods, which is schematically shown on Figure 2. Precisely, the three defining elements of a detection algorithm are reviewed separately. In Section 4, cost functions from the literature are presented, along with the associated signal model and the type of change that can be detected. Whenever possible, theoretical results on asymptotic consistency are also given. Section 5 lists search methods that efficiently solve the discrete optimizations associated with Problem 1 (P1) and Problem 2 (P2). Both exact and approximate methods are described. Constraints on the number of change points are reviewed in Section 6. A summary table of the literature review can be found in Section 7. The last section 8 is dedicated to the presentation of the Python package that goes with this article and propose a modular implementation of all the main approaches described in this article.

3 Evaluation

Change point detection methods can be evaluated either by proving some mathematical properties of the algorithms (such as consistency) in general case, or empirically by computing several metrics to assess the performances on a given dataset.

3.1 Consistency

A natural question when designing detection algorithms is the consistency of estimated change point indexes, as the number of samples TT goes to infinity. In the literature, the “asymptotic setting” is intuitively described as follows: the observed signal yy is regarded as a realization of a continuous-time process on an equispaced grid of size 1/T1/T, and “TT goes to infinity” means that the spacing of the sampling grid converges to 0. Precisely, for all τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], let Y⁡(τ)Y(\tau) denote an ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued random variable such that

yt=Y⁡(t/T)∀t=1,…,T.y_{t}=Y(t/T)\hskip 10.00002pt\forall t=1,\dots,T. (2)

The continuous-time process undergoes K∗K^{*} changes in the probability distribution at the time instants τk∗∈(0,1)\tau^{*}_{k}\in(0,1). Those τk∗\tau^{*}_{k} are related to the change point indexes tk∗t^{*}_{k} through the following relationship:

tk∗=⌊T​τk∗⌋.t^{*}_{k}=\lfloor T\tau^{*}_{k}\rfloor. (3)

Generally, for a given change point index tkt_{k}, the associated quantity τk=tk/T∈(0,1)\tau_{k}=t_{k}/T\in(0,1) is referred to as a change point fraction. In particular, the change point fractions τk∗\tau^{*}_{k} (k=1,…,K∗k=1,\dots,K^{*}) of the time-continuous process YY are change point indexes of the discrete-time signal yy. Note that in this asymptotic setting, the lengths of each regime of yy increase linearly with TT. The notion of asymptotic consistency of a change point detection method is formally introduced as follows.

Definition 1 (Asymptotic consistency)

A change point detection algorithm is said to be asymptotically consistent if the estimated segmentation 𝒯^={t^1,t^2,…}\widehat{\mathcal{T}}=\{\hat{t}_{1},\hat{t}_{2},\dots\} satisfies the following conditions, when T⟶+∞T\longrightarrow+\infty:

  1. (i)

    P⁡(|𝒯^|=K∗)⟶1P(|\widehat{\mathcal{T}}|=K^{*})\longrightarrow 1,

  2. (ii)

    1T​‖𝒯^−𝒯∗‖∞​⟶𝑝​0\frac{1}{T}\left\lVert\widehat{\mathcal{T}}-\mathcal{T}^{*}\right\rVert_{\infty}\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}0,

where the distance between two change point sets is defined by

‖𝒯^−𝒯∗‖∞:=max⁡{maxt^∈𝒯^⁡mint∗∈𝒯∗​|t^−t∗|,maxt∗∈𝒯∗⁡mint^∈𝒯^​|t^−t∗|}.\left\lVert\widehat{\mathcal{T}}-\mathcal{T}^{*}\right\rVert_{\infty}:=\max\ \{\ \max_{\hat{t}\in\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}\ \min_{t^{*}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}}|\hat{t}-t^{*}|,\ \max_{t^{*}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}}\min_{\hat{t}\in\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}|\hat{t}-t^{*}|\ \}. (4)

In Definition 1, the first condition is trivially verified when the number K∗K^{*} of change points is known beforehand. As for the second condition, it implies that the estimated change point fractions are consistent, and not the indexes themselves. In general, distances |t^−t∗||\hat{t}-t^{*}| between true change point indexes and their estimated counterparts do not converge to 0, even for simple models Bai and Perron [2003a], Chakar et al. [2014], Vert and Bleakley [2010], Boysen et al. [2009]. As a result, consistency results in the literature only deal with change point fractions.

3.2 Evaluation metrics

Several metrics from the literature are presented below. Each metric correspond to one of the previously listed criteria by which segmentation performances are assessed. In the following, the set of true change points is denoted by 𝒯∗={t1∗,…,tK∗∗}\mathcal{T}^{*}=\{t^{*}_{1},\dots,t^{*}_{K^{*}}\}, and the set of estimated change points is denoted by 𝒯^={t^1,…,t^K^}\widehat{\mathcal{T}}=\{\hat{t}_{1},\dots,\hat{t}_{\widehat{K}}\}. Note that that the cardinals of each set, K∗K^{*} and K^\widehat{K}, are not necessarily equal.

3.2.1 AnnotationError

The AnnotationError is simply the difference between the predicted number of change points |𝒯^||\widehat{\mathcal{T}}| and the true number of change points |𝒯⋆||\mathcal{T}^{\star}|:

AnnotationError:=|K^−K∗|.\textsc{AnnotationError}:=|\widehat{K}-K^{*}|. (5)

This metric can be used to discriminate detection method when the number of changes is unknown.

3.2.2 Hausdorff

The Hausdorff metric measures the robustness of detection methods Boysen et al. [2009], Harchaoui and Lévy-Leduc [2010]. Formally, it is equal to the greatest temporal distance between a change point and its prediction:

Hausdorff​(𝒯∗,𝒯^):=max⁡{maxt^∈𝒯^⁡mint∗∈𝒯∗​|t^−t∗|,maxt∗∈𝒯∗⁡mint^∈𝒯^​|t^−t∗|}.\textsc{Hausdorff}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}}):=\max\ \{\ \max_{\hat{t}\in\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}\ \min_{t^{*}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}}|\hat{t}-t^{*}|,\ \max_{t^{*}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}}\min_{\hat{t}\in\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}|\hat{t}-t^{*}|\ \}.

It is the worst error made by the algorithm that produced 𝒯^\widehat{\mathcal{T}} and is expressed in number of samples. If this metric is equal to zero, both breakpoint sets are equal; it is large when a change point from either 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} or 𝒯^\widehat{\mathcal{T}} is far from every change point of 𝒯^\widehat{\mathcal{T}} or 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} respectively. Over-segmentation as well as under-segmentation is penalized. An illustrative example is displayed on Figure 3.

3.2.3 RandIndex

Accuracy can be measured by the RandIndex, which is the average similarity between the predicted breakpoint set 𝒯^\widehat{\mathcal{T}} and the ground truth 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} Lajugie et al. [2014]. Intuitively, it is equal to the number of agreements between two segmentations. An agreement is a pair of indexes which are either in the same segment according to both 𝒯^\widehat{\mathcal{T}} and 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} or in different segments according to both 𝒯^\widehat{\mathcal{T}} and 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*}. Formally, for a breakpoint set 𝒯\mathcal{T}, the set of grouped indexes and the set of non-grouped indexes are respectively gr⁡(𝒯)\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal{T}) and ngr⁡(𝒯)\mathrm{ngr}(\mathcal{T}):

gr⁡(𝒯):={(s,t),1≤s<t≤T s.t. s and t belong to the same segment according to 𝒯},ngr⁡(𝒯):={(s,t),1≤s<t≤T s.t. s and t belong to different segments according to 𝒯}.\begin{split}\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal{T})&:=\{(s,t),1\leq s<t\leq T\text{ s.t. }s\text{ and }t\text{ belong to the same segment according to }\mathcal{T}\ \},\\ \mathrm{ngr}(\mathcal{T})&:=\{(s,t),1\leq s<t\leq T\text{ s.t. }s\text{ and }t\text{ belong to different segments according to }\mathcal{T}\ \}.\end{split}

The RandIndex is then defined as follows:

RandIndex​(𝒯∗,𝒯^):=OPEN|gr⁡(𝒯^)∩gr⁡(𝒯∗)|+|ngr⁡(𝒯^)∩ngr⁡(𝒯∗)|)T⁡(T−1).\text{{RandIndex}}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}}):=\frac{|\mathrm{gr}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}})\cap\mathrm{gr}(\mathcal{T}^{*})|+|\mathrm{ngr}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}})\cap\mathrm{ngr}(\mathcal{T}^{*})|)}{T(T-1)}. (6)

It is normalized between 0 (total disagreement) and 1 (total agreement). Originally, RandIndex has been introduced to evaluate clustering methods Boysen et al. [2009], Lajugie et al. [2014]. An illustrative example is displayed on Figure 4.

3.2.4 F1-score

Another measure of accuracy is the F1-Score. Precision is the proportion of predicted change points that are true change points. Recall is the proportion of true change points that are well predicted. A breakpoint is considered detected up to a user-defined margin of error M>0M>0; true positives Tp are true change points for which there is an estimated one at less than MM samples, i.e.

Tp(𝒯∗,𝒯^):={t∗∈𝒯∗|∃t^∈𝒯^s.t.|t^−t∗|<M}.\text{\sc Tp}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}}):=\{t^{*}\in\mathcal{T}^{*}\ |\ \exists\,\hat{t}\in\widehat{\mathcal{T}}\ \ \text{s.t.}\ |\hat{t}-t^{*}|<M\}. (7)

Precision Prec and recall Rec are then given by

Prec​(𝒯∗,𝒯^):=|Tp​(𝒯∗,𝒯^)|/K^andRec​(𝒯∗,𝒯^):=|Tp​(𝒯∗,𝒯^)|/K∗.\text{{\sc Prec}}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}}):=|\text{\sc Tp}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}})|/\widehat{K}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\text{{\sc Rec}}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}}):=|\text{\sc Tp}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}})|/K^{*}. (8)

Precision and Recall are well-defined (ie. between 0 and 1) if the margin MM is smaller than the minimum spacing between two true change point indexes tk∗t^{*}_{k} and tk+1∗t^{*}_{k+1}. Over-segmentation of a signal causes the precision to be close to zero and the recall close to one. Under-segmentation has the opposite effect. The F1-Score is the harmonic mean of precision Prec and recall Rec:

F1-Score​(𝒯∗,𝒯^):=2×Prec​(𝒯∗,𝒯^)×Rec​(𝒯∗,𝒯^)Prec​(𝒯∗,𝒯^)+Rec​(𝒯∗,𝒯^).\text{{F1-Score}}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}}):=2\times\frac{\textsc{Prec}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}})\times\textsc{Rec}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}})}{\textsc{Prec}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}})+\textsc{Rec}(\mathcal{T}^{*},\widehat{\mathcal{T}})}. (9)

Its best value is 1 and its worse value is 0. An illustrative example is displayed on Figure 5.

4 Models and cost functions

This section presents the first defining element of change detection methods, namely the cost function. In most cases, cost functions are derived from a signal model. In the following, models and their associated cost function are organized in two categories: parametric and non-parametric, as schematically shown in Figure 6. For each model, the most general formulation is first given, then special cases, if any, are described. A summary table of all reviewed costs can be found at the end of this section.

4.1 Parametric models

Parametric detection methods focus on changes in a finite-dimensional parameter vector. Historically, they were the first to be introduced, and remain extensively studied in the literature.

4.1.1 Maximum likelihood estimation

Maximum likelihood procedures are ubiquitous in the change point detection literature. They generalize a large number of models and cost functions, such as mean-shifts and scale shifts in normally distributed data Page [1955], Lavielle [1999], Pein et al. [2017], Keshavarz et al. [2018], changes in the rate parameter of Poisson distributed data Ko et al. [2015], etc. In the general setting of maximum likelihood estimation for change detection, the observed signal y={y1,…,yT}y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{T}\} is composed of independent random variables, such that

yt∼∑k=0K∗f(⋅|θk)𝟙(tk∗<t≤tk+1∗)y_{t}\sim\sum_{k=0}^{K^{*}}f(\cdot|\theta_{k})\mathds{1}(t^{*}_{k}<t\leq t^{*}_{k+1}) (M1)

where the tk∗t^{*}_{k} are change point indexes, the f(⋅|θ)f(\cdot|\theta) are probability density functions parametrized by the vector-valued parameter θ\theta, and the θk\theta_{k} are parameter values. In other words, the signal yy is modelled by iid variables with piecewise constant distribution. The parameter θ\theta represents a quantity of interest whose value changes abruptly at the unknown instants tk∗t^{*}_{k}, which are to be estimated. Under this setting, change point detection is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation if the sum of cost V⁡(𝒯,y)V(\mathcal{T},y) is equal to the negative log-likelihood. The corresponding cost function, denoted ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}}, is defined as follows.

Cost function 1 (ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}})

For a given parametric family of distribution densities {f(⋅|θ)|θ∈Θ}\{f(\cdot|\theta)|\theta\in\Theta\} where Θ\Theta is a compact subset of ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p} (for a certain pp), the cost function ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} is defined by

ci.i.d.(ya..b):=−supθ∑t=a+1blogf(yt|θ).c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}}(y_{a..b}):=-\sup\limits_{\theta}\sum_{t=a+1}^{b}\log f(y_{t}|\theta). (C1)

Model M1 and the related cost function ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} encompasses a large number of change point methods. Note that, in this context, the family of distributions must be known before performing the detection, usually thanks to prior knowledge on the data. Historically, the Gaussian distribution was first used, to model mean-shifts Lavielle and Moulines [2000], Sen and Srivastava [1975], Krishnaiah [1988] and scale shifts Ko et al. [2015], Aue and Horvàth [2012], Pein et al. [2017]. A large part of the literature then evolved towards other parametric distributions, most notably resorting to distributions from the general exponential family Maidstone [2013], Fearnhead [2006], Frick et al. [2014].
From a theoretical point of view, asymptotic consistency, as described in Definition 1, has been demonstrated, in the case of a single change point, first with Gaussian distribution (fixed variance), then for several specific distributions, e.g. Gaussian with mean and scale shifts Basseville and Nikiforov [1993], Chen and Gupta [2011a], Keshavarz et al. [2018], Górecki et al. [2018], discrete distributions Lavielle [1999], etc. The case with multiple change points has been tackled later. For certain distributions (e.g. Gaussian), the solutions of the change point detection problems (P1) (known number of change points) and (P2) (unknown number of change points) have been proven to be asymptotically consistent Fu and Curnow [1990]. The general case of multiple change points and a generic distribution family has been addressed decades after the change detection problem has been introduced: the solution of the change point detection problem with a known number of changes and a cost function set to ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} is asymptotically consistent He and Severini [2010]. This is true if certain assumptions are satisfied: (i) the signal follows the model (M1) for a distribution family that verifies some regularity assumptions (which are no different from the assumptions needed for generic maximum likelihood estimation, without any change point) and (ii) technical assumptions on the value of the cost function on homogeneous and heterogeneous sub-signals. As an example, distributions from the exponential family satisfy those assumptions.

Related cost functions.

The general model (M1) has been applied with different families of distributions. We list below three notable examples and the associated cost functions: change in mean, change in mean and scale, and change in the rate parameter of count data.

  • •

    The mean-shift model is the earliest and one of the most studied model in the change point detection literature Page [1955], Chernoff and Zacks [1964], Lorden [1971], Mallows [1973], Sen and Srivastava [1975]. Here, the distribution is Gaussian, with fixed variance. In other words, the signal yy is simply a sequence of independent normal random variables with piecewise constant mean and same variance. In this context, the cost function ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} becomes cL2c_{L_{2}}, defined below. This cost function is also referred to as the quadratic error loss and has been applied for instance on DNA array data Frick et al. [2014] and geology signals Chen and Gupta [2011b].

    Cost function 2 (cL2c_{L_{2}})

    The cost function cL2c_{L_{2}} is given by

    cL2​(ya..b):=∑t=a+1b‖yt−y¯a..b‖22c_{L_{2}}(y_{a..b}):=\sum_{t=a+1}^{b}\left\lVert y_{t}-\bar{y}_{a..b}\right\rVert^{2}_{2} (C2)

    where y¯a..b\bar{y}_{a..b} is the empirical mean of the sub-signal ya..by_{a..b}.

  • •

    A natural extension to the mean-shift model consists in letting the variance abruptly change as well. In this context, the cost function ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} becomes cΣc_{\Sigma}, defined below. This cost function can be used to detect changes in the first two moments of random (not necessarily Gaussian) variables, even though it is the Gaussian likelihood that is plugged in ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} Lavielle [1999], Jandhyala et al. [2013]. It has been applied for instance on stock market time series Lavielle [1999], biomedical data Chen and Gupta [2011b], and electric power consumption monitoring Hébrail et al. [2010].

    Cost function 3 (cΣc_{\Sigma})

    The cost function cΣc_{\Sigma} is given by

    cΣ​(ya..b):=(b−a)​log​detΣ^a..b+∑t=a+1b(yt−y¯a..b)′​Σ^a..b−1​(yt−y¯a..b)c_{\Sigma}(y_{a..b}):=(b-a)\log\det\widehat{\Sigma}_{a..b}+\sum_{t=a+1}^{b}(y_{t}-\bar{y}_{a..b})^{\prime}\widehat{\Sigma}_{a..b}^{-1}(y_{t}-\bar{y}_{a..b}) (C3)

    where y¯a..b\bar{y}_{a..b} and Σ^a..b\widehat{\Sigma}_{a..b} are respectively the empirical mean and the empirical covariance matrix of the sub-signal ya..by_{a..b}.

  • •

    Change point detection has also be applied on count data modelled by a Poisson distribution Chib [1998], Ko et al. [2015]. More precisely, the signal yy is a sequence of independent Poisson distributed random variables with piecewise constant rate parameter. In this context, the cost function ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} becomes cPoissonc_{\mbox{Poisson}}, defined below.

    Cost function 4 (cPoissonc_{\mbox{Poisson}})

    The cost function cPoissonc_{\mbox{Poisson}} is given by

    cPoisson​(ya..b):=−(b−a)​y¯a..b​log⁡y¯a..bc_{\mbox{Poisson}}(y_{a..b}):=-(b-a)\bar{y}_{a..b}\log\bar{y}_{a..b} (C4)

    where y¯a..b\bar{y}_{a..b} is the empirical mean of the sub-signal ya..by_{a..b}.

Remark 1

A model slightly more general than (M1) can be formulated by letting the signal samples to be dependant and the distribution function f(⋅|θ)f(\cdot|\theta) to change over time. This can in particular model the presence of unwanted changes in the statistical properties of the signal (for instance in the statistical structure of the noise Lavielle [1999]). The function f(⋅|θ)f(\cdot|\theta) is replaced in (M1) by a sequence of distribution functions ft(⋅|θ)f_{t}(\cdot|\theta) which are not assumed to be identical for all indexes tt. Changes in the functions ftf_{t} are considered nuisance parameters and only the variations of the parameter θ\theta must be detected. Properties on the asymptotic consistency of change point estimates can be obtained in this context. We refer the reader to Lavielle [1999], Lavielle [2005] for theoretical results.

4.1.2 Piecewise linear regression

Piecewise linear models are often found, most notably in the econometrics literature, to detect so-called “structural changes” Bai [1994], Bai [1995], Bai [1996]. In this context, a linear relationship between a response variable and covariates exists, and this relationship changes abruptly at some unknown instants. Formally, the observed signal yy follows a piecewise linear model with change points located at the tk∗t^{*}_{k}:

∀t,tk∗<t≤tk+1∗,yt=xt′​uk+zt′​v+εt(k=0,…,K∗)\forall\ t,\ t^{*}_{k}<t\leq t^{*}_{k+1},\hskip 10.00002pty_{t}=x_{t}^{\prime}u_{k}+z_{t}^{\prime}v+\varepsilon_{t}\hskip 10.00002pt(k=0,\dots,K^{*}) (M2)

where the uk∈ℝpu_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} and v∈ℝqv\in\mathbb{R}^{q} are unknown regression parameters and εt\varepsilon_{t} is noise. Under this setting, the observed signal yy is regarded as a univariate response variable (ie d=1d=1) and the signals x={xt}t=1Tx=\{x_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} and z={zt}t=1Tz=\{z_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} are observed covariates, respectively ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}-valued and ℝq\mathbb{R}^{q}-valued. In this context, change point detection can be carried out by fitting a linear regression on each segment of the signal. To that end, the sum of costs is made equal to the sum of squared residuals. The corresponding cost function, denoted clinearc_{\mbox{linear}}, is defined as follows.

Cost function 5 (clinearc_{\mbox{linear}})

For a signal yy (response variable) and covariates xx and zz, the cost function clinearc_{\mbox{linear}} is defined by

clinear​(ya..b):=min⁡∑t=a+1bu∈ℝp,v∈ℝq⁡(yt−xt′​u−zt′​v)2.c_{\mbox{linear}}(y_{a..b}):=\min_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{p},v\in\mathbb{R}^{q}}\ \sum_{t=a+1}^{b}(y_{t}-x_{t}^{\prime}u-z_{t}^{\prime}v)^{2}. (C5)

In the literature, Model (M2) is also known as a partial structural change model because the linear relationship between yy and xx changes abruptly, while the linear relationship between yy and zz remains constant. The pure structural change model is obtained by removing the term zt′​vz_{t}^{\prime}v from (M2). This formulation generalizes several well-known models such as the autoregressive (AR) model Angelosante and Giannakis [2012], Bai [2000], multiple regressions Bai [1996], Bai [1997a], etc. A more general formulation of (M2) that can accommodate a multivariate response variable yy exists Qu and Perron [2007], but is more involved, from a notational standpoint.
From a theoretical point of view, piecewise linear models are extensively studied in the context of change point detection by a series of important contributions Bai [1994], Bai [1995], Bai [1996], Bai [1997a], Bai and Perron [1998], Bai [1998], Bai [1999], Bai [2000], Bai and Perron [2003b], Perron [2006], Bai [2010]. When the number of changes is known, the most general consistency result can be found in Bai and Perron [1998]. A multivariate extension of this result has been demonstrated in Qu and Perron [2007]. As for the more difficult situation of an unknown number of changes, statistical tests have been proposed for a single change Bai et al. [1998] and multiple changes Bai [1999]. All of those results are obtained under various sets of general assumptions on the distributions of the covariates and the noise. The most general of those sets can be found in Perron and Qu [2006]. Roughly, in addition to some technical assumptions, it imposes the processes xx and zz to be weakly stationary within each regime, and precludes the noise process to have a unit root.

Related cost functions.

In the rich literature related to piecewise linear models, the cost function clinearc_{\mbox{linear}} has been applied and extended in several different settings. Two related cost functions are listed below.

  • •

    The first one is clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}}, which was introduced in order to accommodate certain noise distributions with heavy tails Bai [1995], Bai [1998] and is defined as follows.

    Cost function 6 (clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}})

    For a signal yy (response variable) and covariates xx and zz, the cost function clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}} is defined by

    clinear,L1​(ya..b):=min⁡∑t=a+1bu∈ℝp,v∈ℝq⁡|yt−xt′​u−zt′​v|.c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}}(y_{a..b}):=\min_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{p},v\in\mathbb{R}^{q}}\ \sum_{t=a+1}^{b}|y_{t}-x_{t}^{\prime}u-z_{t}^{\prime}v|. (C6)

    The difference between clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}} and clinearc_{\mbox{linear}} lies in the norm used to measure errors: clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}} is based on a least absolute deviations criterion, while clinearc_{\mbox{linear}} is based on a least squares criterion. As a result, clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}} is often applied on data with noise distributions with heavy tails Maidstone [2013], Jandhyala et al. [2013]. In practice, the cost function clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}} is computationally less efficient than the cost function clinearc_{\mbox{linear}}, because the associated minimization problem (C6) has no analytical solution. Nevertheless, the cost function clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}} is often applied on economic and financial data Bai [1994], Bai [1995], Bai [1996]. For instance, changes in several economic parameters of the G-7 growth have been investigated using a piecewise linear model and clinear,L1c_{\mbox{linear},L_{1}} Doyle and Faust [2005].

  • •

    The second cost function related to clinearc_{\mbox{linear}} has been introduced to deal with piecewise autoregressive signals. The autoregressive model is a popular representation of random processes, where each variable depends linearly on the previous variables. The associated cost function, denoted cA​Rc_{AR}, is defined as follows.

    Cost function 7 (cA​Rc_{AR})

    For a signal yy and an order p≥1p\geq 1, the cost function cA​Rc_{AR} is defined by

    cA​R​(ya..b):=min⁡∑t=a+1bu∈ℝp⁡‖yt−xt′​u‖2c_{AR}(y_{a..b}):=\min_{u\in\mathbb{R}^{p}}\ \sum_{t=a+1}^{b}\left\lVert y_{t}-x_{t}^{\prime}u\right\rVert^{2} (C7)

    where xt:=[yt−1,yt−2,…,yt−p]x_{t}:=[y_{t-1},y_{t-2},\dots,y_{t-p}] is the vector of lagged samples.

    The piecewise autoregressive model is a special case of the generic piecewise linear model, where the term zt′​vz_{t}^{\prime}v is removed (yielding a pure structural change model) and the covariate signal xx is equal to the signal of lagged samples. The resulting cost function cA​Rc_{AR} is able to detect shifts in the autoregressive coefficients of a non-stationary process Bai [2000], Chakar et al. [2017]. This model has been applied on EEG/ECG time series Qu and Perron [2007], functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) time series Nam et al. [2012] and speech recognition tasks Angelosante and Giannakis [2012].

4.1.3 Mahalanobis-type metric

The cost function cL2c_{L_{2}} (C2), adapted for mean-shift detection, can be extended through the use of Mahalanobis-type pseudo-norm. Formally, for any symmetric positive semi-definite matrix M∈ℝd×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, the associated pseudo-norm ‖⋅‖M\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{M} is given by:

‖yt‖M2:=yt′​M​yt\left\lVert y_{t}\right\rVert^{2}_{M}:=y_{t}^{\prime}My_{t} (10)

for any sample yty_{t}. The resulting cost function cMc_{M} is defined as follows.

Cost function 8 (cMc_{M})

The cost function cMc_{M}, parametrized by a symmetric positive semi-definite matrix M∈ℝd×dM\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}, is given by

cM​(ya..b):=∑t=a+1b‖yt−y¯a..b‖M2c_{M}(y_{a..b}):=\sum_{t=a+1}^{b}\left\lVert y_{t}-\bar{y}_{a..b}\right\rVert^{2}_{M} (C8)

where y¯a..b\bar{y}_{a..b} is the empirical mean of the sub-signal ya..by_{a..b}.

Intuitively, measuring distances with the pseudo-norm ‖⋅‖M\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{M} is equivalent to applying a linear transformation on the data and using the regular (Euclidean) norm ‖⋅‖\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert. Indeed, decomposing the matrix M=U′​UM=U^{\prime}U yields:

‖yt−ys‖M2=‖U​yt−U​ys‖2.\left\lVert y_{t}-y_{s}\right\rVert^{2}_{M}=\left\lVert Uy_{t}-Uy_{s}\right\rVert^{2}. (11)

Originally, the metric matrix MM was set equal to the inverse of the covariance matrix, yielding the Mahalanobis metric Mahalanobis [1936], ie

M=Σ^−1M=\widehat{\Sigma}^{-1} (12)

where Σ^\widehat{\Sigma} is the empirical covariance matrix of the signal yy. By using cMc_{M}, shifts in the mean of the transformed signal can be detected. In practice, the transformation UU (or equivalently, the matrix MM) is chosen to highlight relevant changes. This cost function generalizes all linear transformations of the data samples. In the context of change point detection, most of the transformations are unsupervised, for instance principal component analysis or linear discriminant analysis Hastie et al. [2009]. Supervised strategies are more rarely found, even though there exist numerous methods to learn a task-specific matrix MM in the context of supervised classification Hastie et al. [2009], Xing et al. [2003], Davis et al. [2007]. Those strategies fall under the umbrella of metric learning algorithms. In the change point detection literature, there is only one work that proposes a supervised procedure to calibrate a metric matrix MM Lajugie et al. [2014]. In this contribution, the authors use a training set of annotated signals (meaning that an expert has provided the change point locations) to learn MM iteratively. Roughly, at each step, a new matrix MM is generated in order to improve change point detection accuracy on the training signals. However, using the cost function cMc_{M} is not adapted to certain applications, where a linear treatment of the data is insufficient. In that situation, a well-chosen non-linear transformation of the data samples must be applied beforehand Lajugie et al. [2014].

4.2 Non-parametric models

When the assumptions of parametric models are not adapted to the data at hand, non-parametric change point detection methods can be more robust. Three major approaches are presented here, each based on different non-parametric statistics, such as the empirical cumulative distribution function, rank statistics and kernel estimation.

Signal model.

Assume that the observed signal y={y1,…,yT}y=\{y_{1},\dots,y_{T}\} is composed of independent random variables, such that

yt∼∑k=0K∗Fk​ 1​(tk∗<t≤tk+1∗)y_{t}\sim\sum_{k=0}^{K^{*}}\ F_{k}\ \mathds{1}(t^{*}_{k}<t\leq t^{*}_{k+1}) (M3)

where the tk∗t^{*}_{k} are change point indexes and the FkF_{k} are cumulative distribution functions (c.d.f.​), not necessarily parametric as in (M1). Under this setting, the sub-signal ytk∗..tk+1∗y_{t^{*}_{k}..t^{*}_{k+1}}, bounded by two change points, is composed of iid variables with c.d.f. FkF_{k}. When the FkF_{k} belong to a known parametric distribution family, change point detection is performed with the MLE approach described in Section 4.1.1, which consists in applying the cost function ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}}. However, this approach is not possible when the distribution family is either non-parametric or not known beforehand.

4.2.1 Non-parametric maximum likelihood

The first non-parametric cost function example, denoted cF^c_{\widehat{F}}, has been introduced for the single change point detection problem in Einmahl and McKeague [2003] and extended for multiple change points in Zou et al. [2014]. It relies on the empirical cumulative distribution function, estimated on sub-signals. Formally, the signal is assumed to be univariate (ie d=1d=1) and the empirical cdf on the sub-signal ya..by_{a..b} is given by

∀u∈ℝ,F^a..b​(u):=1b−a​[∑t=a+1b𝟙​(yt<u)+0.5×𝟙​(yt=u)].\forall u\in\mathbb{R},\hskip 10.00002pt\widehat{F}_{a..b}(u):=\frac{1}{b-a}\ \bigg[\sum_{t=a+1}^{b}\mathds{1}(y_{t}<u)+0.5\times\mathds{1}(y_{t}=u)\bigg]. (13)

In order to derive a log-likelihood function that does not depend on the probability distribution of the data, ie the f(⋅|θk)f(\cdot|\theta_{k}), the authors use the following fact: for a fixed u∈ℝu\in\mathbb{R}, the empirical cdf F^\widehat{F} of nn iid random variables, distributed from a certain cdf FF is such that n​F^​(u)∼Binomial​(n,F⁡(u))n\widehat{F}(u)\sim\mbox{Binomial}(n,F(u)) Zou et al. [2014]. This observation, combined with careful summation over uu, allows a distribution-free maximum likelihood estimation. The resulting cost function cF^c_{\widehat{F}} is defined as follows. Interestingly, this strategy was first introduced to design non-parametric two-sample statistical tests, which were experimentally shown to be more powerful than classical tests such as Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Cramér-von Mises Einmahl and McKeague [2003], Zhang [2006].

Cost function 9 (cF^c_{\widehat{F}})

The cost function cF^c_{\widehat{F}} is given by

cF^(ya..b):=−(b−a)∑u=1TF^a..b​(u)​log⁡F^a..b​(u)+(1−F^a..b​(u))​log⁡(1−F^a..b​(u))(u−0.5)​(T−u+0.5)c_{\widehat{F}}(y_{a..b}):=-(b-a)\ \sum_{u=1}^{T}\frac{\widehat{F}_{a..b}(u)\log\widehat{F}_{a..b}(u)+(1-\widehat{F}_{a..b}(u))\log(1-\widehat{F}_{a..b}(u))}{(u-0.5)(T-u+0.5)} (C9)

where the empirical cdf F^a..b\widehat{F}_{a..b} is defined by (13).

From a theoretical point of view, asymptotic consistency of change point estimates is verified, when the number of change points is either known or unknown Zou et al. [2014]. However, solving either one of the detection problems can be computationally intensive, because calculating the value of the cost function cF^c_{\widehat{F}} on one sub-signal requires to sum TT terms, where TT is the signal length. As a result, the total complexity of change point detection is of the order of 𝒪⁡(T3)\mathcal{O}(T^{3}) Zou et al. [2014]. To cope with this computational burden, several preliminary steps are proposed. For instance, irrelevant change point indexes can be removed before performing the detection, thanks to a screening step Zou et al. [2014]. Also, the cost function cF^c_{\widehat{F}} can be approximated, by summing, in (C9), over a few (carefully chosen) terms, instead of TT terms originally Haynes et al. [2017b]. Thanks to those implementation techniques, the cost function cF^c_{\widehat{F}} has been applied on DNA sequences Zou et al. [2014] and heart-rate monitoring signals Haynes et al. [2017b].

4.2.2 Rank-based detection

In statistical inference, a popular strategy to derive distribution-free statistics is to replaced the data samples by their ranks within the set of pooled observations Lévy-Leduc and Roueff [2009], Clemencon et al. [2009], Friedman and Rafsky [1979]. In the context of change point detection, this strategy has first been applied to detect a single change point Lévy-Leduc and Roueff [2009], Lung-Yut-Fong et al. [2012], and then has been extended by Lung-Yut-Fong et al. [2015] to find multiple change points. The associated cost function, denoted crankc_{\mbox{rank}}, is defined as follows. Formally, it relies on the centered ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued “rank signal” r={rt}t=1Tr=\{r_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}, given by

rt,j:=∑s=1T𝟙​(ys,j≤yt,j)−T+12,∀1≤t≤T,∀1≤j≤d.r_{t,j}:=\sum_{s=1}^{T}\mathds{1}(y_{s,j}\leq y_{t,j})\ -\ \frac{T+1}{2},\hskip 10.00002pt\forall 1\leq t\leq T,\ \forall 1\leq j\leq d. (14)

In other words, rt,jr_{t,j} is the (centered) rank of the jthj^{\mbox{th}} coordinate of the ttht^{\mbox{th}} sample, ie yt,jy_{t,j}, among the {y1,j,y2,j,…,yT,j}\{y_{1,j},y_{2,j},\dots,y_{T,j}\}.

Cost function 10 (crankc_{\mbox{rank}})

The cost function crankc_{\mbox{rank}} is given by

crank​(ya..b):=−(b−a)​r¯a..b′​Σ^r−1​r¯a..bc_{\mbox{rank}}(y_{a..b}):=-(b-a)\ \bar{r}_{a..b}^{\prime}\ \widehat{\Sigma}_{r}^{-1}\ \bar{r}_{a..b} (C10)

where the signal rr is defined in (14) and Σ^r∈ℝd×d\widehat{\Sigma}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is the following matrix

Σ^r:=1T​∑t=1T(rt+1/2)′​(rt+1/2).\widehat{\Sigma}_{r}:=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}(r_{t}+1/2)^{\prime}(r_{t}+1/2). (15)

Intuitively, crankc_{\mbox{rank}} measures changes in the joint behaviour of the marginal rank statistics of each coordinate, which are contained in rr. One of the advantages of this cost function is that it is invariant under any monotonic transformation of the data. Several well-known statistical hypothesis testing procedures are based on this scheme, for instance the Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney test Wilcoxon [1945], the Friedman test Lehman and Romano [2006], the Kruskal-Wallis test Kendall [1970], and several others Clemencon et al. [2009], Friedman and Rafsky [1979]. From a computational point of view, two steps must be performed before the change point detection: the calculation of the rank statistics, in 𝒪⁡(d​T​log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(dT\log T) operations, and the calculation of the matrix Σ^r\widehat{\Sigma}_{r}, in 𝒪⁡(d2​T+d3)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}T+d^{3}) operations. The resulting algorithm has been applied on DNA sequences Lung-Yut-Fong et al. [2015] and network traffic data Lévy-Leduc and Roueff [2009], Lung-Yut-Fong et al. [2012].

4.2.3 Kernel-based detection

A kernel-based method has been proposed by Harchaoui and Cappé [2007] to perform change point detection in a non-parametric setting. To that end, the original signal yy is mapped onto a reproducing Hilbert space (rkhs) ℋ\mathcal{H} associated with a user-defined kernel function k⁡(⋅,⋅):ℝd×ℝd→ℝk(\cdot,\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}. The mapping function ϕ:ℝd→ℋ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathcal{H} onto this rkhs is implicitly defined by ϕ⁡(yt)=k⁡(yt,⋅)∈ℋ\phi(y_{t})=k(y_{t},\cdot)\in\mathcal{H}, resulting in the following inner-product and norm:

⟨ϕ⁡(ys)|ϕ⁡(yt)⟩ℋ=k⁡(ys,yt)and‖ϕ⁡(yt)‖ℋ2=k⁡(yt,yt)\left\langle\phi(y_{s})\middle|\phi(y_{t})\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}=k(y_{s},y_{t})\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\left\lVert\phi(y_{t})\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=k(y_{t},y_{t}) (16)

for any samples ys,yt∈ℝdy_{s},y_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The associated cost function, denoted ckernelc_{\mbox{kernel}}, is defined as follows. This kernel-based mapping is central to many machine learning developments such as support vector machine or clustering Schölkopf and Smola [2002], Gretton et al. [2012].

Cost function 11 (ckernelc_{\mbox{kernel}})

For a given kernel function k⁡(⋅,⋅):ℝd×ℝd→ℝk(\cdot,\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}, the cost function ckernelc_{\mbox{kernel}} is given by

ckernel​(ya..b):=∑t=a+1b‖ϕ⁡(yt)−μ¯a..b‖ℋ2c_{\mbox{kernel}}(y_{a..b}):=\sum_{t=a+1}^{b}\left\lVert\phi(y_{t})-\bar{\mu}_{a..b}\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^{2} (C11)

where μ¯a..b∈ℋ\bar{\mu}_{a..b}\in\mathcal{H} is the empirical mean of the embedded signal {ϕ⁡(yt)}t=a+1b\{\phi(y_{t})\}_{t=a+1}^{b} and ‖⋅‖ℋ\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H}} is defined in (16).

Remark 2 (Computing the cost function)

Thanks to the well-known “kernel trick”, the explicit computation of the mapped data samples ϕ⁡(yt)\phi(y_{t}) is not required to calculate the cost function value Celisse et al. [2018]. Indeed, after simple algebraic manipulations, ckernel​(ya..b)c_{\mbox{kernel}}(y_{a..b}) can be rewritten as follows:

ckernel​(ya..b)=∑t=a+1bk⁡(yt,yt)−1b−a​∑s,t=a+1bk⁡(ys,yt).c_{\mbox{kernel}}(y_{a..b})=\sum_{t=a+1}^{b}k(y_{t},y_{t})\ -\ \frac{1}{b-a}\sum_{s,t=a+1}^{b}k(y_{s},y_{t}). (17)
Remark 3 (Intuition behind the cost function)

Intuitively, the cost function ckernelc_{\mbox{kernel}} is able to detect mean-shifts in the transformed signal {ϕ⁡(yt)}t\{\phi(y_{t})\}_{t}. Its use is motivated in the context of Model M3 by the fact that, under certain conditions on the kernel function, changes in the probability distribution coincide with mean-shifts in the transformed signal. This connection has been investigated in several works on kernel methods Sriperumbudur et al. [2008], Schölkopf and Smola [2002], Shawe-Taylor and Cristianini [2004], Gretton et al. [2012]. Formally, let ℙ\mathbb{P} denote a probability distribution defined over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then there exists a unique element μℙ∈ℋ\mu_{\mathbb{P}}\in\mathcal{H} Sriperumbudur et al. [2008], called the mean embedding (of ℙ\mathbb{P}), such that

μℙ=𝔼X∼ℙ​[ϕ⁡(X)].\mu_{\mathbb{P}}=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mathbb{P}}\ [\phi(X)]. (18)

In addition, the mapping ℙ↦μℙ\mathbb{P}\mapsto\mu_{\mathbb{P}} is injective (in which case the kernel is said to be characteristic), meaning that

μℙ=μℚ⟺ℙ=ℚ,\mu_{\mathbb{P}}=\mu_{\mathbb{Q}}\Longleftrightarrow\mathbb{P}=\mathbb{Q}, (19)

where ℚ\mathbb{Q} denotes a probability distribution defined over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. In order to determine if a kernel is characteristic (and therefore, useful for change point detection), several conditions can be found in the literature Sriperumbudur et al. [2008], Schölkopf and Smola [2002], Gretton et al. [2012]. For instance, if a kernel k⁡(⋅,⋅)k(\cdot,\cdot) is translation invariant, meaning that k⁡(ys,yt)=ψ⁡(ys−yt)​∀s,tk(y_{s},y_{t})=\psi(y_{s}-y_{t})\ \forall s,t, where ψ\psi is a bounded continuous positive definite function on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, then it is characteristic Sriperumbudur et al. [2008]. This condition is verified by the commonly used Gaussian kernel. As a consequence, two transformed samples ϕ⁡(ys)\phi(y_{s}) and ϕ⁡(yt)\phi(y_{t}) are distributed around the same mean value if they belong to the same regime, and around different mean-values if they each belong to two consecutive regimes. To put it another way, a signal that follows (M3) is mapped by ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot) to a random signal with piecewise constant mean.

From a theoretical point of view, asymptotic consistency of the change point estimates has been demonstrated for both a known and unknown number of change points in the recent work of Garreau and Arlot [2017]. This result, as well as an important oracle inequality on the sum of cost V⁡(𝒯)V(\mathcal{T}) Arlot et al. [2012], also holds in a non-asymptotic setting. In addition, kernel change point detection was experimentally shown to be competitive in many different settings, in an unsupervised manner and with very few parameters to manually calibrate. For instance, the cost function ckernelc_{\mbox{kernel}} was applied on the Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) data set Harchaoui and Cappé [2007], on a video time series segmentation task Arlot et al. [2012], DNA sequences Celisse et al. [2018] and emotion recognition Cabrieto et al. [2018].

Related cost functions.

The cost function ckernelc_{\mbox{kernel}} can be combined with any kernel to accommodate various types of data (not just ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued signals). Notable examples of kernel functions include Shawe-Taylor and Cristianini [2004]:

  • •

    The linear kernel k⁡(x,y)=⟨x|y⟩k(x,y)=\left\langle x\middle|y\right\rangle with x,y∈ℝdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

  • •

    The polynomial kernel k⁡(x,y)=(⟨x|y⟩+C)d​e​gk(x,y)=(\left\langle x\middle|y\right\rangle+C)^{deg} with x,y∈ℝdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and CC and d​e​gdeg are parameters.

  • •

    The Gaussian kernel k⁡(x,y)=exp⁡(−γ​‖x−y‖2)k(x,y)=\exp(-\gamma\left\lVert x-y\right\rVert^{2}) with x,y∈ℝdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and γ>0\gamma>0 is the so-called bandwidth parameter.

  • •

    The χ2\chi^{2}-kernel k(x,y)=exp(−γ∑i[(xi−yi)2/(xi+yi)])k(x,y)=\exp(-\gamma\sum_{i}[(x_{i}-y_{i})^{2}/(x_{i}+y_{i})]) with γ∈ℝ\gamma\in\mathbb{R} a parameter. It is often used for histogram data.

Arguably, the most commonly used kernels for numerical data are the linear kernel and the Gaussian kernel. When combined with the linear kernel, the cost function ckernelc_{\mbox{kernel}} is formally equivalent to cL2c_{L_{2}}. As for the Gaussian kernel, the associated cost function, denoted crbfc_{\mbox{rbf}}, is defined as follows.

Cost function 12 (crbfc_{\mbox{rbf}})

The cost function crbfc_{\mbox{rbf}} is given by

crbf​(ya..b):=(b−a)−1b−a​∑s,t=a+1bexp⁡(−γ​‖ys−yt‖2)c_{\mbox{rbf}}(y_{a..b}):=(b-a)\ -\ \frac{1}{b-a}\sum_{s,t=a+1}^{b}\exp(-\gamma\left\lVert y_{s}-y_{t}\right\rVert^{2}) (C12)

where γ>0\gamma>0 is the so-called bandwidth parameter.

The parametric cost function cMc_{M} (based on a Mahalanobis-type norm) can be extended to the non-parametric setting through the use of a kernel. Formally, the Mahalanobis-type norm ‖⋅‖ℋ,M\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H},M} in the feature space ℋ\mathcal{H} is defined by

‖ϕ⁡(ys)−ϕ⁡(yt)‖ℋ,M2=(ϕ⁡(ys)−ϕ⁡(yt))′​M​(ϕ⁡(ys)−ϕ⁡(yt))\left\lVert\phi(y_{s})-\phi(y_{t})\right\rVert^{2}_{\mathcal{H},M}=(\phi(y_{s})-\phi(y_{t}))^{\prime}\,M\,(\phi(y_{s})-\phi(y_{t})) (20)

where MM is a (possibly infinite dimensional) symmetric positive semi-definite matrix defined on ℋ\mathcal{H}. The associated cost function, denoted cℋ,Mc_{\mathcal{H},M}, is defined below. Intuitively, using cℋ,Mc_{\mathcal{H},M} instead of cMc_{M} introduces a non-linear treatment of the data samples.

Cost function 13 (cℋ,Mc_{\mathcal{H},M})

For a given kernel function k⁡(⋅,⋅):ℝd×ℝd→ℝk(\cdot,\cdot):\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} and MM a symmetric positive semi-definite matrix defined on the associated rkhs ℋ\mathcal{H}, the cost function cℋ,Mc_{\mathcal{H},M} is given by

cℋ,M​(ya..b):=∑t=a+1b‖ϕ⁡(yt)−μ¯a..b‖ℋ,M2c_{\mathcal{H},M}(y_{a..b}):=\sum_{t=a+1}^{b}\left\lVert\phi(y_{t})-\bar{\mu}_{a..b}\right\rVert^{2}_{\mathcal{H},M} (C13)

where μa..b\mu_{a..b} is the empirical mean of the transformed sub-signal {ϕ⁡(yt)}t=a+1b\{\phi(y_{t})\}_{t=a+1}^{b} and ‖⋅‖ℋ,M\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert_{\mathcal{H},M} is defined in (20).

4.3 Summary table

Reviewed cost functions (parametric and non-parametric) are summarized in Table 1. For each cost, the name, expression and parameters of interest are given.

5 Search methods

This section presents the second defining element of change detection methods, namely the search method. Reviewed search methods are organized in two general categories, as shown on Figure 7: optimal methods, that yield the exact solution to the discrete optimization of (P1) and (P2), and the approximate methods, that yield an approximate solution. Described algorithms can be combined with cost functions from Section 4. Note that, depending on the chosen cost function, the computational complexity of the complete algorithm changes. As a consequence, in the following, complexity analysis is done with the assumption that applying the cost function on a sub-signal requires 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) operations. Also, the practical implementations of the most important algorithms are given in pseudo-code.

5.1 Optimal detection

Optimal detection methods find the exact solutions of Problem 1 (P1) and Problem 2 (P2). A naive approach consists in enumerating all possible segmentations of a signal, and returning the one that minimizes the objective function. However, for (P1), minimization is carried out over the set {𝒯s.t.|𝒯|=K}\{\mathcal{T}\ \mbox{s.t.}\ |\mathcal{T}|=K\} (which contains (T−1K−1){\binom{T-1}{K-1}} elements), and for (P2), over the set {𝒯s.t. 1≤|𝒯|<T}\{\mathcal{T}\ \mbox{s.t.}\ 1\leq|\mathcal{T}|<T\} (which contains ∑K=1T−1(T−1K−1)\sum_{K=1}^{T-1}{\binom{T-1}{K-1}} elements). This makes exhaustive enumeration impractical, in both situations. We describe in this section two major approaches to efficiently find the exact solutions of (P1) and (P2).

5.1.1 Solution to Problem 1 (P1): Opt

In (P1), the number of change points to detect is fixed to a certain K≥1K\geq 1. The optimal solution to this problem can be computed efficiently, thanks to a method based on dynamic programming. The algorithm, denoted Opt, relies on the additive nature of the objective function V⁡(⋅)V(\cdot) to recursively solve sub-problems. Precisely, Opt is based on the following observation:

min|𝒯|=K⁡V⁡(𝒯,y=y0..T)=min⁡∑k=0K0=t0<t1<⋯<tK<tK+1=T⁡c⁡(ytk..tk+1)=mint≤T−K⁡[c⁡(y0..t)+min⁡∑k=0K−1t=t0<t1<⋯<tK−1<tK=T⁡c⁡(ytk..tk+1)]=mint≤T−K⁡[c⁡(y0..t)+min|𝒯|=K−1⁡V⁡(𝒯,yt..T)]\begin{split}\min_{|\mathcal{T}|=K}\ V(\mathcal{T},y=y_{0..T})&=\min_{0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots<t_{K}<t_{K+1}=T}\ \sum_{k=0}^{K}\ c(y_{t_{k}..t_{k+1}})\\ &=\min_{t\leq T-K}\ \bigg[c(y_{0..t})\ +\ \min_{t=t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots<t_{K-1}<t_{K}=T}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\ c(y_{t_{k}..t_{k+1}})\bigg]\\ &=\min_{t\leq T-K}\ \bigg[c(y_{0..t})\ +\ \min_{|\mathcal{T}|=K-1}V(\mathcal{T},y_{t..T})\bigg]\end{split} (21)

Intuitively, Equation 21 means that the first change point of the optimal segmentation is easily computed if the optimal partitions with K−1K-1 elements of all sub-signals yt..Ty_{t..T} are known. The complete segmentation is then computed by recursively applying this observation. This strategy, described in detail in Algorithm 1, has a complexity of the order of 𝒪⁡(K​T2)\mathcal{O}(KT^{2}) Kay and Oppenheim [1993], Bai and Perron [2003c]. Historically, Opt was introduced for a non-related problem Bellman [1955] and later applied to change point detection, in many different contexts, such as EEG recordings Lavielle [2005], Lavielle [1998], DNA sequences Rigaill [2015], Celisse et al. [2018], tree growth monitoring Guédon [2013], financial time-series Lavielle [1999], Perron [2006], radar waveforms Hugueney et al. [2009], etc.

Related search methods.

Several extensions of Opt have been proposed in the literature. The proposed methods still find the exact solution to (P1).

  • -

    The first extension is the “forward dynamic programming” algorithm Guédon [2013]. Contrary to Opt, which returns a single partition, the “forward dynamic programming” algorithm computes the top LL (L≥1L\geq 1) most probable partitions (ie with lowest sum of costs). The resulting computational complexity is 𝒪⁡(L​K​T2)\mathcal{O}(LKT^{2}) where LL is the number of computed partitions. This method is designed as a diagnostic tool: change points present in many of the top partitions are considered very likely, while change points present in only a few of the top partitions might not be as relevant. Thanks to “forward dynamic programming”, insignificant change points are trimmed and overestimation of the number of change point is corrected Guédon [2013], at the expense of a higher computational burden. It is applied on tree growth monitoring time series Guédon [2013] that are relatively short with around a hundred samples.

  • -

    The “pruned optimal dynamic programming” procedure Rigaill [2015] is an extension of Opt that relies on a pruning rule to discard indexes that can never be change points. Thanks to this trick, the set of potential change point indexes is reduced. All described cost functions can be plugged into this method. As a result, longer signals can be handled, for instance long array-based DNA copy number data (up to 10610^{6} samples, with the quadratic error cost function) Rigaill [2015]. However, worst case complexity remains of the order of 𝒪⁡(K​T2)\mathcal{O}(KT^{2}).

5.1.2 Solution to Problem 2 (P2): Pelt

In (P2), the number of changes point is unknown, and the objective function to minimize is the penalized sum of costs. A naive approach consists in applying Opt for K=1,…,KmaxK=1,\dots,K_{\mbox{max}} for a sufficiently large KmaxK_{\mbox{max}}, then choosing among the computed segmentations the one that minimizes the penalized problem. This would prove computational cumbersome because of the quadratic complexity of the resolution method Opt. Fortunately a faster method exists for a general class of penalty functions, namely linear penalties. Formally, linear penalties are linear functions of the number of change points, meaning that

pen​(𝒯)=β​|𝒯|\mbox{pen}(\mathcal{T})=\beta|\mathcal{T}| (22)

where β>0\beta>0 is a smoothing parameter. (More details on such penalties can be found in Section 6.1.) The algorithm Pelt (for “Pruned Exact Linear Time”) Killick et al. [2012] was introduced to find the exact solution of (P2), when the penalty is linear (22). This approach considers each sample sequentially and, thanks to an explicit pruning rule, may or may not discard it from the set of potential change points. Precisely, for two indexes tt and ss (t<s<Tt<s<T), the pruning rule is given by:

if[min𝒯⁡V⁡(𝒯,y0..t)+β​|𝒯|]+c⁡(yt..s)≥[min𝒯⁡V⁡(𝒯,y0..s)+β​|𝒯|]holds,then ​t​ cannot be the last change point prior to ​T.\mbox{if}\quad\bigg[\min_{\mathcal{T}}V(\mathcal{T},y_{0..t})+\beta|\mathcal{T}|\bigg]+c(y_{t..s})\geq\bigg[\min_{\mathcal{T}}V(\mathcal{T},y_{0..s})+\beta|\mathcal{T}|\bigg]\quad\mbox{holds,}\\ \mbox{then }t\mbox{ cannot be the last change point prior to }T. (23)

This results in a considerable speed-up: under the assumption that regime lengths are randomly drawn from a uniform distribution, the complexity of Pelt is of the order 𝒪⁡(T)\mathcal{O}(T). The detailed algorithm can be found in Algorithm 2. An extension of Pelt is described in Haynes et al. [2017a] to solve the linearly penalized change point detection for a range of smoothing parameter values [βmin,βmax][\beta_{\mbox{min}},\beta_{\mbox{max}}]. Pelt has been applied on DNA sequences Hocking et al. [2013a], Maidstone et al. [2017], physiological signals Haynes et al. [2017b], and oceanographic data Killick et al. [2012].

5.2 Approximate detection

When the computational complexity of optimal methods is too great for the application at hand, one can resort to approximate methods. In this section, we describe three major types of approximate segmentation algorithms, namely window-based methods, binary segmentation and bottom-up segmentation. All described procedures fall into the category of sequential detection approaches, meaning that they return a single change point estimate t^(k)\hat{t}^{(k)} (1≤t^(k)<T1\leq\hat{t}^{(k)}<T) at the kk-th iteration. (In the following, the subscript ⋅(k)\cdot^{(k)} refers to the kk-th iteration of a sequential algorithm.) Such methods can be used to solve (approximately) either (P1) or (P2). Indeed, if the number K∗K^{*} of changes is known, K∗K^{*} iterations of a sequential algorithm are enough to retrieve a segmentation with the correct number of changes. If K∗K^{*} is unknown, the sequential algorithm is run until an appropriate stopping criterion is met.

5.2.1 Window sliding

The window-sliding algorithm, denoted Win, is a fast approximate alternative to optimal methods. It consists in computing the discrepancy between two adjacent windows that slide along the signal yy. For a given cost function c⁡(⋅)c(\cdot), this discrepancy between two sub-signals is given by

d⁡(ya..t,yt..b)=c⁡(ya..b)−c⁡(ya..t)−c⁡(yt..b)(1≤a<t<b≤T).d(y_{a..t},y_{t..b})=c(y_{a..b})-c(y_{a..t})-c(y_{t..b})\hskip 10.00002pt(1\leq a<t<b\leq T). (24)

When the two windows cover dissimilar segments, the discrepancy reaches large values, resulting in a peak. In other other words, for each index tt, Win measures the discrepancy between the immediate past (“left window”) and the immediate future (“right window”). Once the complete discrepancy curve has been computed, a peak search procedure is performed to find change point indexes. The complete Win algorithm is given in Algorithm 3 and a schematic view is displayed on Figure 8. The main benefits of Win are its low complexity (linear in the number of samples) and ease of implementation.

In the literature, the discrepancy measure d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) is often derived from a two-sample statistical test (see Remark 4), and not from a cost function, as in (24). However, the two standpoints are generally equivalent: for instance, using cL2c_{L_{2}}, ci.i.d.c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} or ckernelc_{\mbox{kernel}} is respectively equivalent to applying a Student t-test Basseville and Nikiforov [1993], a generalized likelihood ratio (GLR) Chen and Gupta [2011c] test and a kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) test Gretton et al. [2012]. As a consequence, practitioners can capitalize on the vast body of work in the field of statistical tests to obtain asymptotic distributions for the discrepancy measure Gretton et al. [2012], Chen and Gupta [1997], Lung-Yut-Fong et al. [2012], Lévy-Leduc and Roueff [2009], and sensible calibration strategies for important parameters of Win (such as the window size or the peak search procedure). Win has been applied in numerous contexts: for instance, on biological signals Vullings et al. [1997], Brodsky et al. [1999], Harchaoui et al. [2009], Esteller et al. [2001], Karagiannaki et al. [2017], on network data Lévy-Leduc and Roueff [2009], Lung-Yut-Fong et al. [2012], on speech time series Adak [1998], Desobry et al. [2005], Harchaoui et al. [2009] and on financial time series Chen and Gopalakrishnan [1998], Basseville and Nikiforov [1993], Keogh et al. [2004]. It should be noted that certain window-based detection methods in the literature rely on a discrepancy measure which is not related to a cost function, as in (24) Harchaoui et al. [2009], Harchaoui et al. [2008], Liu et al. [2013], Kifer et al. [2004]. As a result, those methods, initially introduced in the online detection setting, cannot be extended to work with optimal algorithms (Opt, Pelt).

Remark 4 (Two-sample test)

A two-sample test (or homogeneity test) is a statistical hypothesis testing procedure designed to assess whether two populations of samples are identical in distribution. Formally, consider two sets of iid ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}-valued random samples {xt}t\{x_{t}\}_{t} and {zt}t\{z_{t}\}_{t}. Denote by ℙx\mathbb{P}_{x} the distribution function of the xtx_{t} and by ℙz\mathbb{P}_{z}, the distribution function of the ztz_{t}. A two-sample test procedure compares the two following hypotheses:

H0:ℙx=ℙzH1:ℙx≠ℙz.\begin{split}H_{0}&:\quad\mathbb{P}_{x}=\mathbb{P}_{z}\\ H_{1}&:\quad\mathbb{P}_{x}\neq\mathbb{P}_{z}.\end{split} (25)

A general approach is to consider a probability (pseudo)-metric d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot) on the space of probability distributions on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Well-known examples of such a metric include the Kullback-Leibler divergence, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD), etc. Observe that, under the null hypothesis, d⁡(ℙx,ℙz)=0d(\mathbb{P}_{x},\mathbb{P}_{z})=0. The testing procedure consists in computing the empirical estimates ℙ^x\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{x} and ℙ^z\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{z} and rejecting H0H_{0} for “large” values of the statistics d⁡(ℙ^x,ℙ^z)d(\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{x},\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{z}). This general formulation relies on a consistent estimation of arbitrary distributions from a finite number of samples. In the parametric setting, additional assumptions are made on the distribution functions: for instance, Gaussian assumption Basseville and Nikiforov [1993], Chen and Gupta [2011b], Chen and Gupta [1997], exponential family assumption Frick et al. [2014], Prescott Adams and MacKay [2007], etc. In the non-parametric setting, the distributions are only assumed to be continuous. They are not directly estimated; instead, the statistics d⁡(ℙ^x,ℙ^z)d(\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{x},\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{z}) are computed Liu et al. [2013], Clemencon et al. [2009], Gretton et al. [2012], Harchaoui et al. [2009].
In the context of single change point detection, the two-sample test setting is adapted to assess whether a distribution change has occurred at some instant in the input signal. Practically, for a given index tt, the homogeneity test is performed on the two populations {ys}s≤t\{y_{s}\}_{s\leq t} and {ys}s>t\{y_{s}\}_{s>t}. The estimated change point location is given by

t^=argmaxt⁡d⁡(ℙ^∙≤t,ℙ^∙>t)\hat{t}=\operatorname{argmax}_{t}\ d(\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\bullet\leq t},\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\bullet>t}) (26)

where ℙ^∙≤t\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\bullet\leq t} and ℙ^∙>t\widehat{\mathbb{P}}_{\bullet>t} are the empirical distributions of respectively {ys}s≤t\{y_{s}\}_{s\leq t} and {ys}s>t\{y_{s}\}_{s>t}.

5.2.2 Binary segmentation

Binary segmentation, denoted BinSeg, is a well-known alternative to optimal methods Sen and Srivastava [1975], because it is conceptually simple and easy to implement Olshen et al. [2004], Chen and Gupta [2011b], Killick et al. [2012]. BinSeg is a greedy sequential algorithm, outlined as follows. The first change point estimate t^(1)\hat{t}^{(1)} is given by

t^(1):=argmin1≤t<T−1⁡c⁡(y0..t)+c⁡(yt..T)⏟V⁡(𝒯={t}).\hat{t}^{(1)}:=\operatorname{argmin}_{1\leq t<T-1}\ \underbrace{c(y_{0..t})+c(y_{t..T})}_{V(\mathcal{T}=\{t\})}. (27)

This operation is “greedy”, in the sense that it searches the change point that lowers the most the sum of costs. The signal is then split in two at the position of t^(1)\hat{t}^{(1)}; the same operation is repeated on the resulting sub-signals until a stopping criterion is met. A schematic view of the algorithm is displayed on Figure 9 and an implementation is given in Algorithm 4. The complexity of BinSeg is of the order of 𝒪⁡(T​log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(T\log T). This low complexity comes at the expense of optimality: in general, BinSeg’s output is only an approximation of the optimal solution. As argued in Bai [1997b], Killick et al. [2012], the issue is that the estimated change points t^(k)\hat{t}^{(k)} are not estimated from homogeneous segments and each estimate depends on the previous ones. Change points that are close are imprecisely detected especially Jandhyala et al. [2013]. Applications of BinSeg range from financial time series Chen and Gupta [1997], Chen and Gupta [2011b], Bai [1997b], Lavielle and Teyssière [2007], Fryzlewicz [2014] to context recognition for mobile devices Himberg et al. [2001] and array-based DNA copy number data Picard et al. [2005], Olshen et al. [2004], Niu and Zhang [2012].

Related search methods.

Several extensions of BinSeg have been proposed to improve detection accuracy.

  • -

    Circular binary segmentation Olshen et al. [2004] is a well-known extension of BinSeg. This method is also a sequential detection algorithm that splits the original at each step. Instead of searching for a single change point in each sub-signal, circular binary segmentation searches two change points. Within each treated sub-segment, it assumes a so-called “epidemic change model”: the parameter of interest shifts from one value to another at the first change point and returns to the original value at the second change point. The algorithm is dubbed “circular” because, under this model, the sub-segment has its two ends (figuratively) joining to form a circle. Practically, this method has been combined with cL2c_{L_{2}} C2, to detect changes in the mean of array-based DNA copy number data Olshen et al. [2004], Lai et al. [2005], Willenbrock and Fridlyand [2005]. A faster version of the original algorithm is described in Venkatraman and Olshen [2007].

  • -

    Another extension of BinSeg is the wild binary segmentation algorithm Fryzlewicz [2014]. In a nutshell, a single point detection is performed on multiple intervals with start and end points that are drawn uniformly. Small segments are likely to contain at most one change but have lower statistical power, while the opposite is true for long segments. After a proper weighting of the change score to account for the differences on sub-signals’ length, the algorithm returns the most “pronounced” ones, ie those that lower the most the sum of costs. An important parameter of this method is the number of random sub-segments to draw. Wild binary search is combined with cL2c_{L_{2}} C2 to detect mean-shifts of univariate piecewise constant signals (up to 2000 samples) Fryzlewicz [2014].

5.2.3 Bottom-up segmentation

Bottom-up segmentation, denoted BotUp, is the natural counterpart of BinSeg. Contrary to BinSeg, BotUp starts by splitting the original signal in many small sub-signals and sequentially merges them until there remain only KK change points. At every step, all potential change points (indexes separating adjacent sub-segments) are ranked by the discrepancy measure d⁡(⋅,⋅)d(\cdot,\cdot), defined in 24, between the segments they separate. Change points with the lowest discrepancy are then deleted, meaning that the segments they separate are merged. BotUp is often dubbed a “generous” method, by opposition to BinSeg, which is “greedy” Keogh et al. [2001]. A schematic view of the algorithm is displayed on Figure 10 and an implementation is provided in Algorithm 5. Its benefits are its linear computational complexity and conceptual simplicity. However, if a true change point does not belong to the original set of indexes, BotUp never considers it. Moreover, in the first iterations, the merging procedure can be unstable because it is performed on small segments, for which statistical significance is smaller. In the literature, BotUp is somewhat less studied than its counterpart, BinSeg: no theoretical convergence study is available. It has been applied on speech time series to detect mean and scale shifts Chen and Gopalakrishnan [1998]. Besides, the authors of Keogh et al. [2001] have found that BotUp outperforms BinSeg on ten different data sets such as physiological signals (ECG), financial time-series (exchange rate), industrial monitoring (water levels), etc.

6 Estimating the number of changes

This section presents the third defining element of change detection methods, namely the constraint on the number of change points. Here, the number of change points is assumed to be unknown (P2). Existing procedures are organized by the penalty function that they are based on. Common heuristics are also described. The organization of this section is schematically shown in Figure 11.

6.1 Linear penalty

Arguably the most popular choice of penalty Killick et al. [2012], the linear penalty (also known as l0l_{0} penalty) generalizes several well-known criteria from the literature such as the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) and the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) Yao [1988], Yao and Au [1989]. The linear penalty, denoted penl0\mbox{pen}_{l_{0}}, is formally defined as follows.

Penalty 1 (penl0\mbox{pen}_{l_{0}})

The penalty function penl0\mbox{pen}_{l_{0}} is given by

penl0​(𝒯):=β​|𝒯|\mbox{pen}_{l_{0}}(\mathcal{T}):=\beta|\mathcal{T}| (28)

where β>0\beta>0 is the smoothing parameter.

Intuitively, the smoothing parameter controls the trade-off between complexity and goodness-of-fit (measured by the sum of costs): low values of β\beta favour segmentations with many regimes and high values of β\beta discard most change points.

Calibration.

From a practical standpoint, once the cost function has been chosen, the only parameter to calibrate is the smoothing parameter. Several approaches, based on model selection, can be found in the literature: they assume a model on the data, for instance (M1), (M2), (M3), and choose a value of β\beta that optimizes a certain statistical criterion. The best-known example of such an approach is BIC, which aims at maximizing the constrained log-likelihood of the model. The exact formulas of several linear penalties, derived from model selection procedures, are given the following paragraph. Conversely, when no model is assumed, different heuristics are applied to tune the smoothing parameter. For instance, one can use a procedure based on cross-validation Arlot and Celisse [2010] or the slope heuristics Birgé and Massart [2007]. In Hocking et al. [2013b], Truong et al. [2017], supervised algorithms are proposed: the chosen β\beta is the one that minimizes an approximation of the segmentation error on an annotated set of signals.

Related penalties.

A number of model selection criteria are special cases of the linear penalty penl0\mbox{pen}_{l_{0}}. For instance, under Model (M1) (iid with piecewise constant distribution), the constrained likelihood that is derived from the BIC and the penalized sum of costs are formally equivalent, upon setting c=ci.i.d.c=c_{\mbox{i.i.d.}} and pen=penBIC\mbox{pen}=\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC}}, where penBIC\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC}} is defined as follows.

Penalty 2 (penBIC\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC}})

The penalty function penBIC\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC}} is given by

penBIC​(𝒯):=p2​log⁡T​|𝒯|\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC}}(\mathcal{T}):=\frac{p}{2}\log T\ |\mathcal{T}| (29)

where p≥1p\geq 1 is the dimension of the parameter space in (M1).

In the extensively studied model of an univariate Gaussian signal, with fixed variance σ2\sigma^{2} and piecewise constant mean, the penalty penBIC\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC}} becomes penL2\mbox{pen}_{L_{2}}, defined below. Historically, it was one of the first penalties introduced for change point detection Schwarz [1978], Yao [1988].

Penalty 3 (penBIC,L2\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC},L_{2}})

The penalty function penBIC,L2\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC},L_{2}} is given by

penBIC,L2​(𝒯):=σ2​log⁡T​|𝒯|.\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{BIC},L_{2}}(\mathcal{T}):=\sigma^{2}\log T\ |\mathcal{T}|. (30)

where σ\sigma is the standard deviation and TT is the number of samples.

In the same setting, AIC, which is a generalization of Mallows’ CpC_{p} Mallows [1973], also yields a linear penalty, namely penAIC,L2\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{AIC},L_{2}}, defined as follows.

Penalty 4 (penAIC,L2\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{AIC},L_{2}})

The penalty function penAIC,L2\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{AIC},L_{2}} is given by

penAIC,L2​(𝒯):=σ2​|𝒯|.\mbox{pen}_{\mbox{AIC},L_{2}}(\mathcal{T}):=\sigma^{2}\ |\mathcal{T}|. (31)

where σ\sigma is the standard deviation.

6.2 Fused lasso

For the special case where the cost function is cL2c_{L_{2}}, a faster alternative to penl0\mbox{pen}_{l_{0}} can be used. To that end, the l0l_{0} penalty is relaxed to a l1l_{1} penalty Harchaoui and Lévy-Leduc [2010], Vert and Bleakley [2010]. The resulting penalty function, denoted penl1\mbox{pen}_{l_{1}}, is defined as follows.

Penalty 5 (penl1\mbox{pen}_{l_{1}})
